I'm wondering if it's worth refactoring classical mechanics into structures based onHamiltonian systems, Newtonian systems, and the Lagrangian systems.

This might be a good project for an undergraduate or a group of undergraduates, if anyone is one or knows anyone that might be interested in doing it.
Sounds like an interesting project. It reminds me that there are some interesting topics in Landau's textbook on classical mechanics that might also be suitable for undergraduates.

Hi there, I would argue that mechanics as Arnold describes it in his mathematical methods is better for the foundations of Physlib. A quick comparison of the two:

L&L:
Starting with least action in generalised coordinates (q,q˙)(q, \dot q)(q,q˙​), they later use the Galilean principle and the homogeneity and isotropy of space and time to fix the form of the Lagrangian. Conservation of energy, momentum, and angular momentum are then derived one by one. Configuration space is never given and we just assume the existence of some coordinates. Even if we wanted to state Noether's theorem in this approach, symmetries would just be specific transformations of coordinates (e.g. a shift by a vector a⃗\vec{a}a or a rotation by δφ⃗\delta\vec{\varphi}δφ​).

Arnold:
Space-time is an affine space that has a Galilean structure. The Lagrangian is L:TM→RL : TM \to \RL:TM→R, where MMM is the configuration manifold, and the Euler-Lagrange equation comes from variations of curves γ\gammaγ on MMM. Noether then becomes a statement about a one-parameter group of diffeomorphisms preserving LLL.

Why?

  • It is already asked for; for example: "A proper formalisation should include the geometric properties of the state space via manifolds and tangent bundles."
  • One Noether: what I don't really like about L&L is how they figure out different conservation laws. Instead of doing all that work, we just prove Noether's theorem once on a manifold and base everything on that. It is therefore better for reuse.
  • Coordinates are painful in proofs (example): in Lean, it is easier to prove something based on a more general structure than to artificially create coordinates and show that everything is invariant under a change of them. It would save time and nerves for anyone building other APIs on top of this or developing it further.

How I see it:
I believe that Arnold should give the definitions and L&L the content. We should define things as in Arnold and prove them as he does, but build an API somewhat following L&L. Then we'll be both general and useful elsewhere in Physlib, while staying welcoming to people who want to contribute in a more L&L style or use it in their projects.

If others agree, I will start the formalization efforts/write a roadmap on how we are to do this. I am open to collaboration on this.

Hi @Michal Mogielnicki , what you're suggesting makes alot of sense, but I feel this might be the rough route that is being built up in the classical harmonic geometric folder, following this nice reference. Though there is work still left to be done completing the geometric formulation for the classical harmonic oscillator and then generalize these patterns for classical mechanics as a whole (and it would be very exciting if you can lead on this :smile:).

I think Joseph is more so suggesting that the form that this work should be arranged based on Hamiltonian, Newtonian, and Lagrangian systems. For eg. a possible folder structure could be like below 

Physlib/ClassicalMechanics/
├── ConfigurationSpace/
│
├── Lagrangian/
│
├── HamiltonianMechanics/
│
├── PointParticle/
│   └── NewtonianSystem/
(deleted)

Agree with everything said above.

I think

I believe that Arnold should give the definitions and L&L the content. We should define things as in Arnold and prove them as he does, but build an API somewhat following L&L. Then we'll be both general and useful elsewhere in Physlib, while staying welcoming to people who want to contribute in a more L&L style or use it in their projects.

Seems like a very nice approach. I think the key here should be to have enough API that one can still do classical mechanics without knowing what a tangent bundle is.
I think the first step of this process should be working out what the key types look like. @Michal Mogielnicki is this something you think you could have a look at, if you have time?

Thanks @Joseph Tooby-Smith and @Nathaneal Sajan for the responses. Yes, I'll have a look, go through the existing geometric folders and draft the types. I'm also happy to lead the implementation afterwards.

I opened #1824 for Lagrangian systems on smooth manifolds. I'm also writing a general roadmap for the refactor. Where should it go? The API maps/a doc/a thread here/some 3rd party?

Also, please let me know if I should fully migrate to the .md maps.
API-map.yaml for now if that is ok, we can migrate them over to .md files when that transition is done. But these API maps are generally where they should go. I added a couple of comments.

Just opened PR#1843 for review. This time very few definitions and mainly API building, so the review should be lighter.

Should I split the PR into multiple or keep it as one (around 1700 LOC)?
Hi, I have not looked at your PR, but generally 1700 lines is very large for a PR, smaller more focused PRs are easier to review and also get merged much faster :)
Kk. I'll think of how to split and update you here once I do it
@Michal Mogielnicki In addition to this, we currently have a number of PRs which need reviewing. Any help with this will mean we can get this classical mechanics results in quicker.
You can use this view to see which PRs ready to review :)
@Michal Mogielnicki would it be possible to add + expand upon the API-map.md (now we have migrated over) for these Lagrangian system results?
Sure thing. Will do
I'll work on it + other ones for a few days and put them as a separate PR on top of the 5th one
Maybe you could add this as a commit to Physlib#1863

I'll have to be a bit less active later today/tomorrow (still responding to reviews/doing light fixes, but you can prioritize others), so I'd prefer to do it later (maybe for one of the next ones).

Is there some specific one (map) that you find to be the best one so far that I should get inspiration from?
I would look at the new changes in Physlib#1882, given the .md versions are still new, there is likely not a concrete best example yet. But the new things in that PR is similar to what I would expect
Thank you. I'll take my time to read it and draft the mechanics ones in a similar format
